subject: Medicine
summary: Alzheimer disease is the commonest cause of progressive dementia in older adults, characterized by memory loss, executive dysfunction and neuropsychiatric changes. Diagnosis relies on clinical criteria supported by imaging and biomarkers.

sections.p: A neurodegenerative disorder causing gradual decline in cognition and function, diagnosed by the NIA‑AA criteria: insidious onset, progressive course, and impairment in at least two cognitive domains, with biomarkers (CSF Aβ42, tau, PET) supporting AD pathology.
b: Clinical criteria focus on history, exam, and functional impact
Biomarkers increase diagnostic certainty but are not mandatory

t.b: How severe is the cognitive impairment? Scores <24 suggest moderate‑to‑severe dementia.
Is there cortical atrophy or ventricular enlargement? Diffuse medial temporal lobe atrophy supports AD.
Does the biomarker profile indicate AD pathology? Low Aβ42 and high tau are typical; if unavailable, rely on clinical criteria.

sections.p: The Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) and Global Deterioration Scale (GDS) are used to stage disease from mild (CDR 1) to severe (CDR 3).
b: Stage guides treatment intensity and care planning
Mild stage: preserved ADLs, early memory loss

sections.p: Most cases are sporadic, linked to age, APOE ε4, and vascular risk factors. Familial early‑onset disease (<65 y) is due to APP, PSEN1/2 mutations.
b: Sporadic AD ≈ 90 % of cases
Early‑onset AD ≈ 5‑10 % and autosomal dominant

sections.p: Gradual memory loss for recent events, difficulty finding words, disorientation, impaired judgment, and later neuropsychiatric symptoms (depression, agitation).
b: Early episodic memory loss is the hallmark
Executive dysfunction appears as disease progresses

sections.p: Combine bedside cognition testing with imaging and, where possible, fluid biomarkers to confirm AD and exclude reversible causes.
b: Rule out vitamin B12 deficiency, thyroid disease, depression
Consider HIV or neurosyphilis in younger patients

t.b: Are there reversible metabolic or infectious contributors? Abnormal results prompt specific treatment.
Is there significant atrophy or alternative pathology? CT can show ventricular enlargement and rule out mass lesions.

sections.p: Rapid decline, new focal neurological signs, seizures, or severe neuropsychiatric agitation require urgent evaluation for alternative diagnoses or complications.
b: Sudden worsening may indicate stroke, infection, or medication side‑effects
Aspiration pneumonia is a common cause of death

sections.p: Treat underlying reversible factors, then use symptomatic disease‑modifying agents (acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, NMDA‑receptor antagonist) and non‑pharmacologic support.
b: Donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine improve cognition modestly
Memantine helps moderate‑to‑severe stages
Avoid anticholinergics and sedatives that worsen cognition

sections.p: Regular review every 6‑12 months to monitor cognition, function, medication side‑effects, and caregiver burden. Lifestyle measures (exercise, Mediterranean diet, blood pressure control) lower risk.
b: Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus to prevent pneumonia
Encourage social engagement to delay functional loss

sections.p: Vascular dementia, Lewy body dementia, frontotemporal dementia, normal‑pressure hydrocephalus, and depression can mimic AD.
b: Vascular dementia shows stepwise decline and focal deficits
Lewy body dementia has visual hallucinations and parkinsonism

sections.p: Normal MMSE early in disease, normal MRI in very early AD, and low CSF tau in some patients can give false reassurance.
b: Rely on longitudinal assessment, not a single test
Consider clinical context when biomarkers are borderline

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening of cognition, new focal neurological signs, seizures, severe agitation, or inability to care for basic needs

faq.a: No cure exists; treatment aims to slow decline and improve quality of life.

faq.q: Is Alzheimer disease only a disease of old age?
faq.a: Most cases occur after 65 y, but early‑onset familial forms can appear before 50 y.
They increase synaptic acetylcholine, modestly improving memory and daily functioning.

exam: Describe the core clinical criteria for diagnosing Alzheimer disease.
Explain how the Clinical Dementia Rating scale stages disease severity.
List two pharmacologic agents used in Alzheimer disease and their rationale.
